{{Short description|Same digit count as prime factorization}}
[[File:Composite number Cuisenaire rods 10.svg|thumb|Demonstration, with [[Cuisenaire rods]], that the [[composite number]] 10 is equidigital: 10 has two digits, and 2 × 5 has two digits (1 is excluded)]]

In [[number theory]], an '''equidigital number''' is a [[natural number]] in a given [[radix|number base]] that has the same number of digits as the number of digits in its [[prime factorization]] in the given number base, including [[Exponentiation|exponents]] but excluding exponents equal to 1.<ref name="Darling102">{{cite book |title=The universal book of mathematics: from Abracadabra to Zeno's paradoxes |last=Darling |first=David J. |year=2004 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=978-0-471-27047-8 |page=102 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nnpChqstvg0C&pg=PA102 }}</ref> For example, in [[base 10]], 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 10 (2 × 5) are equidigital numbers {{OEIS|id=A046758}}. All [[prime number]]s are equidigital numbers in any base.

A number that is either equidigital or [[frugal number|frugal]] is said to be ''economical''.

==Mathematical definition==
Let <math>b > 1</math> be the number base, and let <math>K_b(n) = \lfloor \log_{b}{n} \rfloor + 1</math> be the number of digits in a natural number <math>n</math> for base <math>b</math>. A natural number <math>n</math> has the prime factorisation
: <math>n = \prod_{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}} p^{v_p(n)}</math>
where <math>v_p(n)</math> is the [[p-adic valuation|''p''-adic valuation]] of <math>n</math>, and <math>n</math> is an '''equidigital number''' in base <math>b</math> if
: <math>K_b(n) = \sum_{{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}}} K_b(p) + \sum_{{\stackrel{p^2 \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}}} K_b(v_p(n)).</math>

==Properties==
*Every [[prime number]] is equidigital. This also [[mathematical proof|proves]] that there are infinitely many equidigital numbers.
